questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Within Europe and the Erasmus program I found Warsaw to be one of the most different and interesting places in terms of culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My great experience does not relate to my academic outcome at all. The courses were often chaotic, unorganised and on a lower level than I expected.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy, even though I often struggled when it came to University of Warsaw. For a handfull of courses they didn't have descriptions on the course or the syllabus etc., which University of Copenhagen demanded in order to accept the courses as replacements for my obligatory courses.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I recieved a lot of assistance and information about study life, the city, housing etc. Both from the university and the local Erasmus network. Still I missed assistance with the courses and having them accepted. It was pretty stressfull as my OLA was only completed very late and therefore late before I recieved the Erasmus grant.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Student dormitories.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Only a very scaled down kitchen, where you had to bring everything (pots, pans etc.) yourself. It worked, but it was basically just 10 gas burners.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is a good opportunity because it is cheap and accesible, but you have to be a person who can deal with living in a small room togehter with a person you don't know. You don't really have privacy, so if you need that on a weekly basis it is worth it to find a place with your own room.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My university had a lot of Erasmus students, which meant that the courses we were supposed to take were Erasmus courses with only Erasmus students. But since I had obligatory courses I had to cover, I had to register for regular courses in order to cover it. This meant that I fell a little bit outside the system and the process became complicated.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was a first-come-first-served system of the Erasmus courses. This part worked well, but since I needed regular courses I had to email all the professors from the courses I wanted to get personal permission to join the courses. After this permission I then had to email my faculty coordinator with screenshots of the emails from the professors before they officially could register me. To top it off this also could only happen after the application proces of both Erasmus and regular students was concluded. This meant that I was put back in line in both cases. I had to wait to register for the few Erasmus courses I had room for, because I had to wait to know my schedule with regular courses. This left me with only the Erasmus courses that still had room.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I emailed my faculty and my Erasmus coordinator a lot, but often felt like my problems fell between two chairs.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the end the success criteria was to cover all my obligatory courses. In this regard it ended in a successful way, but I would have like to be able to choose some elective courses that interested me more and not just some I had to take to fill up my schedule after I was put back in line by the system.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patient and don't hesitate to write emails to people if you are in doubt.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic level for some of the courses was extremely low. Often also unstructured and with now clear explanation of what was expected, how we passed the exam, how we were graded, what we were supposed to take away from classes and what the syllabus was.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: A part from a few exceptions very low. Even from some of the MA courses I learned about thing I had learned about before going to university. For a lot of the courses you passed by giving a presentation to the rest of the class and not having too much absence. In these cases the teacher often didn't seem to care too much and around 80% would get the best grade without much effort.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Not at all. I had 10 different courses at the same time. All with a professor in small classes. The idea is good but the professors lacked basic teaching skills.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Economics of the European Integration, Political Institutions in the EU countries, Decision-Making Procedures in the EU, Who runs the World? Girls? Gender & World Politics, Comparative Politics, European Primary and Secondary Law, European Institutions, Comparative Political Systems I, Religion and Politics in Orthodox World, Ukraine: Culture and Identity.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
"European Primary and Secondary Law": the professor was extremely good, structured and engaged. Made the courses very interesting.
"Religion and Politics in Orthodox World" and "Ukraine: Culture and Identity": the two courses were similar and had the same professor, who was very engaged and nerdy about her field. Also two themes that you wouldn't often have the possibility to dig into to.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It turned out to be very expensive to travel 'green'. At all times it would have been cheaper to take a plane than the bus/train, but since I wanted to travel green I ended up spending a lot of money on transportation. Especially around Christmas and New Years where I went home to my family. Here the cheapest tickets ended up costing me more than 2000kr. to get back and fourth.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
In general the pricelevel of groceries etc. Of course it was still cheaper than Denmark, but it was higher than expected from Warsaw and "Eastern Europe" beacuse of the heavy inflation and housing crisis the last two years.
Cultural stuff was supprisingly cheap. Theathers, cinemas, concerts, museums and art all had huge student discounts which gave a lot of opportunities.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Especially the local Erasmus Student Network offered weekly events of various charachter all along the semester.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of different things. Some hosted by the institutions, but in general just huge student discounts on cultural activities, let alone a catalogue of sports activities at the university you could sign up for.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The cultural ones. Warsaw is rich on theathers, museums, concerts and art at a very high level and available at low prices.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I was at a handfull of weekend trips to other places in Poland. In all cases the places we visited was very different from Warsaw, so I highly recommend exploring the country. The regional trains are also very cheap with student discount. I can recommend Lublin in the East, Bielsko-Biala and Krakow to the South and Gdansk to the North. Especially I recommend Zakopane: a city/area in the mountains close to the Slovakian border. You can ski in the winter and hike for the rest of the year in beautiful nature.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Not too hard, but it also helped a lot to have a lot of other Erasmus students in the same situation as you to share your experiences with.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: To join regular courses so you meet non-Erasmus students. If you live in a dorm you automatically also get to talk to other people. The Erasmus Student Network volunteers are often local as well and are always happy to talk.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The amount of hierarchy and respect for authorities. You didn't get a personal bond with your professors or the personel in the dorm because there was a very defined hierarchy.
Also the amount of patriotism/nationalism among the Polish people. It was hard to get used to that these thing might mean different things in this context than my own back in Denmark.
The lack of trust in authorities (the police for example) from normal people.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The co-excisting of Soviet culture (architecture, state-funded cafeterias to secure cheap food) and a more Western culture with diversity, political awareness etc. Both contains things that is specific for Warsaw and not the rest of Poland.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Even if you don't get a huge academic outcome you still get to experience Polish culture and have a pretty good idea about Polish culture and the Polish people, which might confront some stereotypes about Eastern Europe and Post-Soviet states.
- Warsaw is an amazing and interesting city with a lot of possibilities. Take your time to explore concerts, museums, art etc. You will experience some things that you are not able to elsewhere. Also, the areas of the city is very different. I encourage you to spend days to visit other parts of the city.
- Exchange can be tough socially. A million things is happening all the time with hundreds of new people. Try to avoid FOMO as much as possible. Take your breaks and find time to do things on your own. Try to find 'your people' instead of just a big group drinking beer every night. It is nice and fun to party, but remember that this is not where actual friendships are made. It isnice if you make friends for life, but even if you want stay in touch it's also valuable that you shared experiences, fun and conversations in an exchange bubble for 4-5 months.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Mostly the information I gave about registration for regular courses and housing at the dormitory.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To be very upfront in terms of making friendships. Everyone is in the same situation, so it's perfectly normal to ask someone out on a friend-date. It can be a very rewarding situation to be in. I also allowed myself to make friends I usually wouldn't have made at home. Because I knew the friendships didn't have to last forever, but it was enough that it was an interesting relation. This is meant as a good thing, even though it might not sound like it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To have privacy and relax because I lived in the dorm in a small room with a guy who was always there. I struggled to recharged my batteries.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
